awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I:  New Paradigm for Combination Drug Optimization and Discovery
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (STTR) Phase I project is in addressing directly the challenge of optimizing the use and discovery of drug combinations. Effective combination drug therapies optimize the therapeutic effects of these drugs and minimize harmful and/or uncomfortable side effects. Many diseases, including cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, and life-threatening infections, are treated by drugs used in combination. Amazingly, the use of these drug combination is guided by analytical methods that are over 100 years old. Researchers have developed the first components of a new analytical toolkit for combination drug discovery and development across a range of disease indications. This STTR Phase 1 research project will enable the commercialization of this toolkit by discovering how to harness the power of artificial intelligence (AI) to sift through a range of existing (and future) laboratory and clinical data to find the drug combinations that work best. The combination drug toolkit may create significant value for its customers by (1) improving target selection, (2) reducing the number of drug development programs that fail, (3) increasing the efficiency of clinical trials data analysis, and (4) extending the patent life of important drugs with new viable combinations.

The proposed project seeks to leverage improvements in quantitative understanding of drug – drug synergy to overcome challenges associated with the optimization and discovery of combination drug therapies. The Multidimensional Synergies of Combination (MuSyC) algorithm is valued as an improvement in understanding drug – drug synergy by rigorously defining synergy of efficacy and synergy of potency and extracting these different synergies from experimental data sets. The proposed research seeks to innovate the means of data production and integration across diverse data sources and merge this with additional relevant databases and clinical data to create an effective analytical toolkit for optimizing all stages of combination drug research and development. The research plan consists of an experimental track and a computational track. The experimental track will use the MuSyC algorithm to inform experimental design and high-throughput data collection for three use cases of considerable clinical relevance. In parallel, the Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning approaches will be used to integrate diverse data sets with the MuSyC algorithm to predict synergies of combinations. The data track and the AI-track will then be merged to provide proof-of-concept for an AI-enabled MuSyC toolkit for optimizing combination drug use and discovery.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Treating disease with a combination of drugs is a cornerstone of modern medicine, including treatments for cancer and infectious diseases. Combining drugs can potentially improve treatment effectiveness, overcome resistance, or reduce the amount of medication required. However, determining whether a combination provides a meaningful benefit remains a significant challenge in pharmaceutical research. Traditional analytical approaches frequently rely on a single measure of drug "synergy," which may not adequately distinguish different types of benefits or provide the information needed to guide subsequent development decisions.

With support from the National Science Foundation's Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program, Duet Biosystems and Northeastern University worked to show that there is a better way to quantify the benefits of drug combinations. Duet Biosystems Multi-dimensional Synergy of Combinations algorithm, aka MuSyC, provides a new way for biomedical researchers to develop and optimize the use of drugs in combination. Unlike current, conventional approaches that compress understanding of drug interactions into a single synergy score, MuSyC distinguishes between changes in the amounts of drugs needed to achieve an effect (i.e., potency) versus the maximum achievable effect (i.e., efficacy). MuSyC also identifies circumstances in which adding another agent provides no measurable benefit. These distinctions can help researchers understand the contribution of each drug, evaluate the potential value of a combination, and determine which experiments or development activities should follow.

To explore whether the MuSyC algorithm can reduce the development time needed to bring a novel drug combination and increase the success rate for such combinations, we evaluated MuSyC across three distinct biological applications: lung cancer, pain management, and antibacterial drug discovery. Each application tested MuSyC's ability to characterize experimental results, assess uncertainty, and provide scientifically interpretable information supporting development decisions.

Cancer treatment. We evaluated combinations of the chemotherapeutic agents cisplatin and etoposide in the context of SCLC. The cisplatin-etoposide combination is the standard of care for treating -cell lung cancer (SCLC). MuSyC analysis of quantitative dose response experiments data and found that, under the conditions tested, the combination provided no measurable improvement beyond the more effective individual drug. This finding highlighted an emerging view in oncology that drug-drug synergy is quite nuanced. Specifically, the effect of drug combination in tissue culture or in animal models may not reflect their success in clinical trials. New computations tools, such as MuSyC are, needed to better model how drug combinations work in patients.

Pain Management. Opioid addiction is a challenge to effective pain management. Duet Biosystems and Northeastern University researchers used MuSyC to understand cross talk between cannabinoid and opioid receptor signaling. Together we found that novel drugs that stimulate cannabinoid receptors greatly accentuate the effect of opioids. We discovered combinations of the cannabinoid modulators with opioids that would clinicians to achieve the same amount of pain management while using lower doses opioids. This demonstrated the MuSyC's applicability across a range of clinically relevant applications and suggested potential ‘spin-off’ approaches to pain management.

Antibacterial combinations. Antibiotic resistance is an increasing challenge. When treating multi-drug resistant bacteria using drug combinations is becoming the standard of care. The need to discover new, effective combinations is increasingly urgent. Duet Biosystems and Northeastern University researchers evaluated six combinations of antibiotics with other pharmacologic agents. MuSyC identified three combinations exhibiting potentially beneficial interactions, distinguishing two that increased antibiotic potency from one that improved maximum bacterial growth inhibition. The analysis also identified combinations that did not demonstrate a meaningful benefit under the tested conditions. These results illustrated how a single analytical framework can generate different, actionable conclusions, helping researchers prioritize combinations and determine which follow-up experiments are warranted.

We demonstrated that MuSyC can characterize diverse experimental datasets and distinguish among favorable interactions and findings requiring additional investigation. The studies also established that practical commercialization requires more than accurate mathematical modeling. Reliable application depends on appropriate experimental design, standardized data preparation, robust model fitting, assessment of uncertainty, and clear interpretation of results. Importantly, these findings demonstrated the potential to translate analytical results into specific development actions, including advancing promising combinations, deprioritizing unproductive approaches, and identifying experiments needed to resolve uncertainty.

Duet supported the initial development of DeepMuSyC, an artificial intelligence capability designed to predict drug-combination responses using information about individual drugs and their biological effects. This separately funded effort extended the quantitative foundation established by MuSyC and complemented the experimental and analytical work conducted during Phase I. This work supports the potential for AI-assisted prioritization of combinations before complete experimental screening, although further prospective validation is required. Future work will focus on standardizing and scaling quantitative analysis, further validating AI-assisted prediction, and integrating these capabilities with other pharmacologic evidence to support more transparent and reproducible development decisions.

The NSF funded work supports our goal of helping pharmaceutical researchers identify promising drug combinations, reduce unproductive experimentation, and accelerate the evaluation of novel therapies.
